tip: 'Ber-' + a noun can mean going to get it: 'obat' (medicine) gives 'berobat', to seek treatment. 'Tempat berobat' = the place you go to get treated.
'KRIS' ('kelas rawat inap standar') is replacing the old 'kelas' 1–3 – one standard room class for all.
'Hari itu juga' = that very same day. 'Juga' after a time phrase adds 'right then'.
'Siapa pun' = anyone at all: 'jangan kasih tahu siapa pun' = don't tell anyone. 'Pun' strengthens.
'Ter-' often marks accidents: 'tertelan' = accidentally swallowed (by the machine), 'tertinggal' = left behind.
'Benar-benar' = really, truly: 'benar-benar masuk' = has really arrived. Doubling the adjective intensifies it.
'Kena' = to get hit with (bad things): 'kena denda' = get fined, 'kena flu' = catch the flu.
'Makan waktu' = to take time (lit. eat time): 'prosesnya makan waktu lima hari' = it takes five days.
'Antara lain' introduces a partial list – 'among others': 'syarat antara lain akta kelahiran dan kartu keluarga' means those plus more not named.
'Daftar ulang' = re-register to claim your seat ('ulang' = again). Miss it and the spot is gone.
'Pas foto' = ID photo; sizes are in cm: 'tiga kali empat' = 3x4. Standard for most forms.
'Tujuh belasan' is 'tujuh belas' (17) plus '-an' – the suffix turns the date into the whole event: any August 17 festivity is 'acara tujuh belasan'.
'Dirgahayu' = 'long live', banner language: 'Dirgahayu Republik Indonesia'.
Before a verb, 'baru' means 'only just', not 'new': 'baru belajar puasa' = is only just learning to fast. As 'new', 'baru' follows its noun instead.
'Cair' is literally 'liquid'; for money it means paid out: 'THR ayah cair' = Dad's bonus came through. Salaries and funds 'cair' when they land.
'Mohon maaf lahir dan batin' is the fixed 'Lebaran' formula: 'forgive my wrongs, outward and inner' – 'lahir' is the outward side, 'batin' the inner.
'Arus mudik' = the outbound exodus; 'arus balik' = the return wave. News-speak every 'mudik' season.
The 'ter-' in 'terjual' means it happened with no doer named: 'habis terjual' is literally 'used up, got sold' – sold out.
The 'angpao' rule: married adults give the red envelopes, the unmarried receive – which is why the card says 'belum menikah'. Marriage flips your role.
'Cuti bersama' is government-set shared leave glued onto a holiday – the whole 'kantor' usually closes on those dates whether you asked for leave or not.
Spoken time uses 'jam': 'jam dua belas malam' = 12 at night. 'Pukul' is for formal announcements.
Doubling inside 'ber-...-an' makes it mutual: 'bermaaf-maafan' = forgive one another. 'Saling berkunjung' uses 'saling' = each other for the same job.
The birthday custom runs in reverse: 'yang berulang tahun wajib mentraktir' – the birthday person treats everyone else, not the other way around.
'Dulu' after a verb = 'first': 'dikocok dulu sebelum diminum' = shaken first before drinking.
A doubled adjective can mean 'in that manner': 'dioleskan tipis-tipis' = spread on thinly.
Adding '-kan' can mean 'have it done': 'periksa' = examine, 'periksakan ke dokter' = have it examined by a doctor. You arrange it, someone else performs it.
'Tolong' + verb = please (asking for help): 'tolong panggil ambulans' = please call an ambulance.
Numbers you dial are read digit by digit: 112 = 'satu satu dua', never 'seratus dua belas'.
The '-lah' ending softens a command: 'turunlah lewat tangga' = do go down the stairs.
'Untung' at the start of a sentence = luckily: 'untung ada tetangga' = luckily there was a neighbor.
